records.title: CVT Transmission Shudder and Failure
records.description: The Spark's CVT (continuously variable transmission) develops shuddering during acceleration, particularly between 20-40 mph. The transmission can eventually fail completely, leaving the vehicle unable to move. The issue is linked to belt wear and pulley degradation.
records.solution: Minor shudder may be temporarily improved with CVT fluid change using genuine GM fluid. Severe cases require transmission replacement as the CVT is not practically rebuildable.
symptoms: Hesitation when pulling away from stops
Check engine light with transmission codes

citations.title: GM Preliminary Information PIP5581 - CVT7 Shudder on Launch or Low-Speed Acceleration

records.title: Ignition Coil and Spark Plug Failure
records.description: The 1.4L engine in the Spark is prone to premature ignition coil failure, often causing misfires and rough running. Individual coil packs fail due to heat soak in the tight engine bay. Spark plugs also wear faster than the recommended interval suggests.
records.solution: Replace the failed ignition coil pack. Recommended to replace all four coils and spark plugs at once since labor overlaps and remaining coils are likely near end of life.
symptoms: Reduced power and poor fuel economy

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: 4L60E Transmission 3-4 Clutch Failure / Loss of 3rd & 4th
records.description: The 4L60E automatic behind the half-ton Suburban is notorious for burning up the 3-4 clutch pack. The 3-4 apply circuit is long and loses pressure as valve-body bores wear, so the clutches overheat and glaze. Symptoms are slipping in 3rd/4th, a jump from 2nd straight to 4th, or a sudden loss of 3rd and 4th (RPM flares, no forward pull in higher gears while reverse and low gears still work). On 2004+ units the input drum can also crack, and the pot-metal sun-gear shell ("sun shell") strips teeth, causing loss of reverse.
records.solution: Rebuild or replace the transmission. A proper rebuild must go beyond soft parts: install a hardened sun shell, address worn valve-body/pump bores (Sonnax/TransGo shift-kit correction), quality 3-4 clutches, and a fresh input drum. Add an auxiliary cooler and keep fluid fresh to prolong life. Budget for a full remanufactured unit if the case/drum is damaged.
symptoms: Slipping or RPM flare in 3rd/4th gear

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: 5.7L Vortec CSFI 'Spider' Poppet Injector Failure
records.description: GMT400-era Vortec V8s use a Central Sequential Fuel Injection (CSFI) 'spider' assembly with poppet-valve nozzles inside the intake. The poppet valves clog with carbon or the nozzle seats fail, so they leak/dribble fuel instead of atomizing. This causes hard starting, misfires, rough idle, hesitation, poor fuel economy, and often a raw-gasoline smell; failing poppets can dump fuel into a cylinder. A very high-demand repair for high-mileage 1996-2000 Suburbans.
records.solution: Replace the spider/CSFI unit. The preferred upgrade is the later MFI (multi-port) spider with individual nozzles instead of poppets (GM MFI conversion assembly, e.g. AC Delco 217-3411 / GM 12574601), which bolts to 1996-2001 Vortec engines with no modifications and cures the poppet problem. Replace fuel filter and inspect the pressure regulator at the same time.
symptoms: Loss of power and poor fuel economy

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: AFM/DFM Lifter Failure (5.3L/6.2L V8)
records.description: The Active Fuel Management (AFM) and Dynamic Fuel Management (DFM) systems on the 5.3L and 6.2L V8 engines deactivate cylinders to save fuel by collapsing hydraulic valve lifters. These lifters have a complex locking pin mechanism that fails, causing the lifter to collapse and the affected cylinder to misfire. A collapsed lifter can also damage the camshaft lobe it rides on, turning a $300 lifter into a $3,000 camshaft and lifter replacement. The issue affects 2007+ Suburbans and is one of the most complained-about GM V8 problems. GM switched from 4-cylinder AFM to 17-pattern DFM in 2019, but lifter failures continue.
records.solution: Replace the failed lifter(s) and inspect the camshaft for damage. A single-side lifter replacement (one bank of 8 lifters) costs $1,500-$2,500 including labor. If the camshaft is damaged, add $500-$1,000 for a new cam and installation. Many owners opt to replace all 16 lifters and delete the AFM/DFM system with an AFM delete kit ($200-$400) and a custom tune that disables cylinder deactivation. This eliminates the root cause but requires a tuner ($400-$600). GM range device ($300) is a plug-in alternative that keeps all cylinders active without a tune.
symptoms: Engine misfire on one or more cylinders
Ticking or tapping noise from engine
Check engine light with misfire codes
P0300 random misfire or specific cylinder misfire code

citations.title: GM Service Bulletin 15-06-01-002O - Engine Misfire/Tick Noise and DTC P0300

records.title: Dashboard Cracking
records.description: The dashboard on 2007-2014 Suburbans develops extensive cracking across the top surface due to UV exposure and heat cycling. The dashboard material shrinks and hardens over time, causing deep fissures that spread across the full width of the dash. The cracking is worst in southern and southwest states with intense sun exposure, but affects vehicles nationwide. GM was the subject of multiple class-action lawsuits over this defect across the GMT900 platform (Tahoe, Suburban, Silverado, Yukon). The cracked dashboard is a cosmetic and resale value issue.
records.solution: GM settled a class-action lawsuit and offered reimbursement for dashboard replacements on some model years — check if your VIN qualifies by contacting GM customer service. A new OEM dashboard costs $1,500-$3,000 installed. More practical solutions include a Coverlay molded dashboard cover ($200-$350) that fits over the cracked dash and looks nearly factory, or a DashMat fabric cover ($50-$100). Some owners have the dashboard professionally recovered at an upholstery shop ($500-$1,200). Always use a windshield sunshade when parked to slow further deterioration.
symptoms: Deep cracks spreading across dashboard surface
Pieces of dashboard material breaking off

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Erratic Fuel Gauge / Fuel Level Sensor Failure
records.description: The in-tank fuel level sending unit reads incorrectly on these Suburbans - the gauge sticks, bounces, reads full or empty regardless of actual level, or drops to E with a low-fuel light on a full tank. The failure is the sensor card/wiper: aggressive sulfur and ethanol in modern fuel corrode the resistor contacts and wear the float-arm 'teeth,' so the signal to the PCM is erratic. RepairPal lists this as a recognized Suburban 1500 problem.
records.solution: Replace the fuel level sensor, which on most GMT800 tanks means dropping the tank and swapping the sending unit or the complete fuel pump/sender module (AC Delco module or a GM level-sensor kit). Before full replacement, some owners clean the contacts by running a bottle of Techron/fuel-system cleaner, which can restore an intermittently-dirty sender. Verify the tank ground and connector while the tank is down.
symptoms: Fuel gauge stuck, bouncing, or pinned
Reads empty on a full tank / full on empty
Low-fuel light on with plenty of fuel
Gauge slow to update after fill-up

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Exhaust Manifold Bolt Breakage / Cold-Start Tick
records.description: The exhaust manifold retaining bolts fatigue and snap from repeated heat-cycling on the Vortec V8s. As clamp load is lost the manifold-to-head seal leaks, producing a ticking/chuffing 'exhaust leak' noise that is loudest on cold start and quiets as the metal expands and warms. Owners often smell exhaust near the wheel well. Broken bolts are frequently found rusted/seized in the head, complicating the repair.
records.solution: Replace the broken manifold bolts (often requires drilling/extracting a bolt seized in the cylinder head) and a new manifold gasket. Many owners upgrade to a kit with longer bolts plus spacers or a manifold clamp/bracket to reduce fastener stress and stop recurrence. Warped manifolds should be resurfaced or replaced.
symptoms: Exhaust smell near engine bay/wheel well

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Front Wheel Hub Bearing Failure (ABS Light)
records.description: The sealed front wheel bearing/hub assemblies on 4WD Suburbans wear out and are a top high-mileage complaint. Because the ABS wheel-speed sensor is integrated into the hub, a failing bearing (or a failed sensor) commonly triggers the ABS and traction/StabiliTrak warning lights along with a cyclic humming/growling that changes with speed and cornering load. The hub is a non-serviceable sealed unit.
records.solution: Replace the complete front hub/bearing assembly (6-lug 4WD units such as GM 15042868 / 15104582, cross-ref Timken/Moog 515058). Use a quality name-brand or GM hub - cheap units and their ABS sensors fail quickly. Torque the axle nut and the three hub bolts to spec and clear the ABS codes after replacement.
symptoms: Noise changes when turning left vs right
ABS and traction-control warning lights on
Play/wobble at the wheel when jacked up

citations.title: NHTSA Recall 05V-379 / GM 05068B - Front Wheel Speed Sensor Corrosion

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Dash)
records.description: The plastic gears inside the HVAC blend/mode door actuators strip out, so the door can't move. The classic symptom is a repetitive clicking or tapping from behind the dash (near the glovebox/center) when starting the truck or changing temperature, plus one side blowing hot while the other blows cold, or air stuck on defrost/one temperature. Mode-door actuators fail the same way but click when switching vent/floor.
records.solution: Replace the failed actuator (GM 89018365 / AC Delco 15-73989 / Dorman 604-106 for the main blend actuator). After installation, run the HVAC recalibration by pulling the HVAC fuse for ~60 seconds and cycling the key so the module relearns the door stops. Identify which actuator by whether the click tracks with temperature (blend) or airflow direction (mode).
symptoms: One side hot, other side cold
Temperature or vent selection won't change
Air stuck on defrost or one setting

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Instrument Cluster Gauge Failure (Stepper Motor)
records.description: The 2003-2006 (GMT800) analog cluster uses tiny Switec/Juken X27.168 stepper motors to drive each gauge needle. These motors wear and lose steps, so the speedometer, tachometer, fuel, and temperature gauges stick, read wildly wrong, sweep erratically, or drop to zero while driving. It usually starts with one gauge (often speedometer or fuel) and spreads to the rest. Dim or dark odometer/PRNDL segments from cracked circuit-board solder joints are a related failure. GM issued an extended warranty on affected clusters that has since expired.
records.solution: Repair or replace the cluster. The permanent fix is to replace the failed X27.168 stepper motors (sold in 6-motor repair kits with upgraded motors and backlight bulbs) and re-flow the board solder, or install a remanufactured cluster. The cluster is a ~1-hour DIY removal (7mm socket + trim tool); a rebuilt/repaired unit keeps the original odometer mileage. Many owners send the cluster to a rebuild service for $150-250.
symptoms: Fuel gauge jumping or reading empty when full
All gauges sweep and freeze on startup

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Knock Sensor Connector Corrosion (P0327/P0332)
records.description: On Gen III/IV Vortec V8s the two knock sensors sit in the lifter valley beneath the intake manifold, under a plastic cover. Water and debris collect in the valley and corrode the sensor connectors and wiring; the factory connectors also embrittle from heat. The result is an intermittent knock-sensor signal that sets P0327 (Bank 1) and/or P0332 (Bank 2), illuminating the check engine light. GM settled a class-action over the design.
records.solution: Remove the intake manifold, replace both knock sensors (AC Delco 213-3521 / GM 12570125) AND the knock-sensor wiring harness (GM 12601822), reseal the valley cover, and add dielectric grease to the connectors. Replacing only the sensors without the harness often leaves the fault. Kits bundling both sensors, the harness, and an intake gasket set are widely sold.

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Rear A/C Line Corrosion and Leak
records.description: The Suburban has a rear A/C system with refrigerant lines that run the full length of the vehicle underneath, exposed to road salt, debris, and moisture. These aluminum and steel lines corrode through, especially at the connections and where the lines are clamped to the frame. When a line corrodes through, the entire A/C system loses its refrigerant charge and both front and rear A/C stop working. The rear lines are particularly vulnerable because they are in the splash zone behind the rear wheels. This is a widespread issue in northern salt-belt states.
records.solution: Replace the corroded rear A/C lines ($200-$600 for parts). Labor is 2-4 hours ($200-$500) as the lines must be routed under the vehicle. The entire A/C system must be evacuated before repair and recharged afterward ($100-$200 for evacuation and recharge). Also replace the receiver/drier ($30-$60) whenever the system has been open to the atmosphere. Some shops fabricate replacement lines from copper tubing and compression fittings, which resists corrosion better than the OEM steel lines. Apply undercoating or wax coating to new lines to prevent future corrosion.
symptoms: Front and rear A/C both stop cooling
A/C works after recharge but fails again quickly
Visible corrosion or green residue on A/C lines under vehicle
Oily refrigerant stain on A/C line connections
Hissing sound from under vehicle when A/C is on

records.title: Reduced Engine Power / Throttle Body (TAC) Failure
records.description: The electronic (drive-by-wire) throttle system triggers a 'Reduced Engine Power' / 'Engine Power Is Reduced' limp mode that sharply limits acceleration and speed - dangerous when it strikes in traffic. The cause is usually the throttle actuator control (TAC): worn internal throttle-body sensors/motor, or a broken/chafed wire in the harness a few inches from the throttle-body connector. Correlation codes P2135 and TAC-performance code P1516 are typical.
records.solution: Inspect the throttle-body connector and wiring first (the wires break near the plug); repair chafed wiring before replacing parts. If the throttle body itself is worn, replace it (AC Delco 217-3151 / GM 12570800) and relearn the idle. Cleaning a carbon-fouled throttle body resolves milder cases. Some model years had extended special coverage on the accelerator-pedal/TAC system - check with a dealer.
symptoms: 'Reduced Engine Power' message and limp mode
Check engine light with throttle codes

citations.title: GM Preliminary Information PIP4578B - Throttle-Body Carbon and Idle Learn

records.title: Steering Column Lock and Click Noise
records.description: The 2015+ Suburban uses an electronic steering column lock that can malfunction, causing a clicking noise from the steering column, failure to recognize the key fob, or preventing the vehicle from starting. The electronic lock module replaces the traditional key-cylinder lock and communicates with the body control module (BCM) to verify the key fob is present before allowing the engine to start. When the lock module fails, it may click repeatedly without unlocking, or it may not engage at all, leaving the steering unlocked even when the vehicle is off.
records.solution: The steering column lock actuator module needs replacement ($150-$400 for parts, $200-$400 labor). The module is located inside the steering column and requires partial disassembly to access. A scan tool is needed to program the new module to the BCM after installation. In some cases, a BCM software update at the dealer resolves the clicking without hardware replacement. If the vehicle will not start due to a failed lock module, a tow to the dealer is required — there is no manual override.
symptoms: Rapid clicking noise from steering column
Vehicle will not start — "Steering Column Lock" message
Key fob not detected despite fresh battery
Steering wheel does not lock when vehicle is off

citations.title: GM Preliminary Information PIT5452 - Upper Steering Column Click While Turning

records.title: Steering Intermediate Shaft Clunk
records.description: A widely reported clunk/knock felt in the steering wheel and column, most noticeable turning at low speed over bumps or during small back-and-forth steering inputs. The telescoping upper intermediate steering shaft loses its internal lubrication and the splines take up play with a metallic clunk. GM documented it in TSB 00-02-35-003M covering 2000-2006 Suburban/Tahoe.
records.solution: Per the TSB the permanent fix is to replace the upper intermediate steering shaft with the improved design (GM P/N 19153614) - the newer shaft is sealed and cannot be re-greased. Temporary relief is possible by packing the splines with grease, but the noise returns; replacement is the real fix. On 2002+ trucks a steering-column lock tool is needed to keep the column from rotating during the job.
symptoms: Clunk/knock felt in steering wheel over bumps
Notchy or popping feel during slow turns
Play when rocking the steering wheel

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Transfer Case Fluid Leak
records.description: The transfer case on the 4WD Suburban develops fluid leaks from the front and rear output shaft seals, the input shaft seal, or the case halves where the case splits. The NP246 (half-ton) and NP261/NP263 (heavy-duty) transfer cases all share this tendency. Low transfer case fluid causes the internal clutch pack to overheat and burn, leading to expensive internal damage. The rear output seal is the most common leak source, and the leak often drips onto the exhaust, creating a burning fluid smell. Many owners do not realize the transfer case has its own fluid that needs periodic changing.
records.solution: Replace the leaking seal(s) — the rear output shaft seal is $10-$20 for the part and 1-2 hours of labor ($100-$250). The front output seal is similar but harder to access. If the case halves are leaking, resealing requires splitting the case ($400-$800 labor). Check the transfer case fluid level every oil change and change the fluid every 50,000 miles with the GM-specified Auto-Trak II (NP246) or DEXRON VI (NP261/NP263). Low fluid is a transfer case killer — check before it is too late.
symptoms: Fluid dripping from transfer case area
Burning fluid smell from under vehicle
Grinding or whining noise from transfer case
Fluid stain on driveway near center of vehicle

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Vortec Intake Manifold Gasket Leak (Vacuum/Oil)
records.description: The Gen III/IV LS-based Vortec V8s use a plastic (nylon) intake manifold with molded silicone/rubber gaskets. With heat cycling and age the gaskets harden and crack, creating an unmetered vacuum leak that leans out the mixture and can weep oil at the manifold-to-head sealing surface. Owners report rough/lean idle, hesitation, and lean-bank misfire codes. Not to be confused with the earlier 5.7 CSFI issue - this is the plastic-manifold sealing failure common across the GMT800 run.
records.solution: Replace the intake manifold gaskets (AC Delco/Fel-Pro MS98003 series 8-piece set) and inspect the plastic manifold for warping/cracks around the ports; badly warped manifolds should be replaced. Clean the sealing surfaces, torque the manifold bolts in sequence to spec, and clear codes. It is a good time to also address the knock sensors and harness that live in the valley underneath.
symptoms: Check engine light for lean condition

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Vortec V8 Cold-Start Piston Slap
records.description: Early GMT800 Vortec V8s are known for cold-start 'piston slap' - a brief knock/rattle for the first several seconds to a minute after a cold start that fades as the engine warms. The early LS-series pistons had short skirts and extra bore clearance, so the piston rocks in the cylinder until thermal expansion takes up the gap. GM considered it a cosmetic characteristic and issued no recall; it typically does not affect longevity or performance.
records.solution: Usually no repair is needed if the noise is brief and drivability is normal - keep up with on-schedule 5W-30 synthetic oil changes and a full crankcase to minimize it. Persistent, worsening, or hot-running knock should be diagnosed to rule out a real bearing/rod knock; genuine excessive slap is only cured by an engine/short-block rebuild with new pistons.
symptoms: Knock/rattle for seconds after cold start
No loss of power or oil pressure

citations.title: GM Service Bulletin 01-06-01-028C - Engine Knock on Cold Start

records.title: 4L60E Automatic Transmission 3-4 Clutch Failure (Loss of 3rd/4th Gear)
records.description: The 4L60E 4-speed automatic behind the Vortec V8s is the single most common major failure on high-mileage Tahoes. The 3-4 clutch pack is the known weak point: its friction plates burn up, and the truck suddenly slips or drops out of 3rd and 4th gear (RPMs flare with no acceleration), leaving effectively only 1st and 2nd. Later-production units (roughly 2004+) used thinner/cheaper clutch material and tend to fail earlier. Contributing factors include worn shift solenoids, a leaking valve body/accumulator, TCC solenoid failure, and neglected/burnt fluid. Many owners hit this between 120k-180k miles.
records.solution: Verify fluid level and color first (burnt/dark red = internal wear). Scan for solenoid/pressure codes. A slipping 3-4 clutch means an internal rebuild or a remanufactured unit: budget for a rebuild with a heavy-duty (Alto/Raybestos) 3-4 clutch pack and updated Sonnax valve-body parts, or install a reman 4L60E. Address the TCC/shift solenoids and a fresh filter at the same time. Preventive fluid+filter service every ~50k miles and an added transmission cooler markedly extend life on these trucks.

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: 4L60E transmission loss of reverse (cracked sun shell / worn lo-reverse clutches)
records.description: The 4L60E automatic behind the 5.7L is prone to losing reverse (and sometimes 2nd) as it ages. The classic root cause is the reaction sun shell ("sunshell") cracking or stripping its splines, along with worn lo-reverse clutches. Slipping typically appears first in reverse and worsens until reverse is gone entirely; a fractured sunshell can also take out 2nd. The 1995 model is a transition year whose transmission does not directly interchange, so a rebuild is generally the only route for those trucks.
records.solution: Rebuild the 4L60E with an upgraded hardened sun shell and fresh lo-reverse/reverse clutch pack. Diagnose first with a line-pressure test in reverse to separate hydraulic (valve body/servo) from mechanical (sunshell/clutch) causes. Keep fluid and filter serviced to prolong life.
symptoms: Slipping in reverse, then no reverse
Clunk or vibration when backing up
Loss of 2nd gear in some cases

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: 5.3L Vortec Excessive Oil Consumption (Low-Tension Rings / PCV)
records.description: Gen IV 5.3L V8s burn oil at an abnormal rate, frequently far worse than GM's own 1 qt / 2,000 mi 'acceptable' threshold. Three compounding root causes: (1) low-tension piston rings that fail to scrape oil from the cylinder walls; (2) the Active Fuel Management (AFM) oil-pressure relief valve in the valley that sprays a jet of oil directly at the deactivated cylinders' piston skirts, overloading the already-leaking rings; and (3) an early PCV routing in the valve cover that pulls liquid oil into the intake to be burned. Owners see the low-oil light between changes, fouled spark plugs on AFM cylinders (commonly cyl 1 and 7), and eventual carbon-clogged rings. Distinct from AFM lifter collapse — this is oil burning, not a lifter failure.
records.solution: Address the PCV path first: install GM's updated valve cover / AFM oil-deflector-equipped cover per the oil-consumption TSB, and replace fouled plugs. To stop the AFM oil spray, either install an AFM/DoD delete (disabler module as a stopgap, or full delete with a non-AFM valley cover and standard lifters/plate) or clean/replace carboned rings if damage exists. Use the correct 0W-20/5W-30 dexos oil and check level frequently. Confirm consumption with a documented oil-consumption test before major internal work.
symptoms: Low oil level / light between changes
Blue smoke on startup or acceleration

citations.title: GM Service Bulletin 10-06-01-008M - AFM Engine Oil Consumption

records.title: 6.2L L87 Rod-Bearing Engine Failure (Recall 25V-274)
records.description: L87 6.2L V8s built March 1, 2021 through May 31, 2024 can suffer sudden rod-bearing failure and engine seizure with loss of propulsion. GM attributes it to supplier manufacturing/quality issues — sediment/debris left on connecting rods and in crankshaft oil galleries plus out-of-spec dimensions — that starve and pound the rod bearings. NHTSA safety recall 25V-274 (April 2025) covers 44,802 Tahoes among ~600k GM full-size trucks/SUVs; GM logged over 14,000 field complaints and a dozen alleged crashes/injuries. NHTSA has since opened follow-up query RQ26001 into failures on engines outside the recall and on some units that failed after the dealer remedy.
records.solution: Follow recall 25V-274: dealer inspects the engine and replaces it if it fails inspection; vehicles that pass receive higher-viscosity 0W-40 dexos oil, a new oil filter, and an updated oil-fill cap specifying the new viscosity. Owners hearing a knock, seeing low oil pressure, or getting loss-of-propulsion warnings should stop driving and contact a dealer. Out-of-warranty engine replacement absent recall coverage runs well into five figures — verify VIN eligibility with GM before paying.

citations.title: NHTSA Recall 25V-274 - L87 Connecting-Rod and Crankshaft Manufacturing Defects
NHTSA Recall Query RQ26-001 - Post-Remedy L87 Engine Failures
NHTSA Engineering Analysis EA25-007 - L87 Failures Outside Recall Scope

records.title: Blower Motor Resistor Failure (Heater/AC Fan Only Works on High)
records.description: On manual-A/C Tahoes the blower motor resistor (that controls fan speeds 1-4) is a very common failure. Classic symptom: the fan works only on the highest setting (High bypasses the resistor) while the lower speeds are dead; sometimes all speeds quit, and a burning-plastic smell can appear at the resistor connector. Root cause is often an aging blower motor drawing excess amperage and a corroded/overheated connector, which cooks the resistor.
records.solution: Replace the resistor located on the HVAC box in the passenger footwell. OEM: ACDelco 15-81086 (GM 89019088); common aftermarket: Dorman 973-405. Because the melted connector is usually the real culprit, install a resistor kit that INCLUDES a new pigtail/harness (many kits bundle it). If the blower motor itself is noisy or drawing high current, replace it too or the new resistor will burn out again. An easy DIY: a few screws, ~$25-80 part.
symptoms: Fan works only on high speed
Lost one or more middle fan speeds

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Brake line and fuel line rust-through corrosion (Salt Belt)
records.description: The steel brake and fuel lines on GMT400 Tahoes corrode and rupture, especially in road-salt states. Brake lines rust from the outside in and can burst suddenly, producing a sinking pedal and severe loss of stopping power, frequently with no warning light. NHTSA received ~890 brake-pipe corrosion complaints on GM full-size trucks/SUVs; its formal probe (EA11-001) centered on 1999-2003 models but the same AlGal-coated Bundy lines and failure mode apply to earlier GMT400s, with the great majority of failures in Salt Belt states. Fuel lines rot in the same environment, typically around the tank, leaking raw fuel.
records.solution: Inspect all steel lines; replace corroded brake and fuel lines, ideally with corrosion-resistant (stainless or coated/PVF) pre-bent line sets. Bleed brakes thoroughly after brake-line replacement. NHTSA guidance for at-risk trucks is to periodically wash the underbody to remove salt.
symptoms: Brake fluid leak / loss of stopping power
Fuel smell and fuel leak near the tank

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Broken Exhaust Manifold Bolts (Startup Ticking)
records.description: The exhaust manifold-to-head bolts on GM small-block V8s fatigue and snap after years of heat cycling, most often the front and rear bolts on each manifold. The result is a distinctive tick/puff that is loudest on a cold start and quiets as the engine warms and the manifold expands to seal. It is extremely common on higher-mileage trucks and worse in road-salt regions where the bolt heads corrode. Left alone it causes an exhaust leak, can burn the manifold gasket, and may set O2/fuel-trim codes.
records.solution: Replace the broken bolts and manifold gaskets, torquing new hardware to spec. Heads that snapped flush usually require an extractor or weld-a-nut removal; Dorman and similar makers also sell exhaust-manifold repair clamp kits (e.g. Dorman exhaust manifold hardware kit) that bolt into an unused hole and clamp the manifold down without extracting a seized stud. Use updated bolts and new gaskets to prevent recurrence.

records.title: A/C Condenser Cracking / Refrigerant Leak
records.description: The factory A/C condenser on K2XX-platform Tahoes cracks from thermal-stress cycling, typically where the tubes meet the core, allowing refrigerant to escape. The result is A/C that blows warm again a season or two after a recharge. It was widespread enough that GM issued Special Coverage Adjustment 17336 extending A/C-condenser coverage to 5 years / 60,000 miles, and a 2018 class action targeted 2015-2017 Tahoe/Suburban/Yukon. Simply adding refrigerant is only a temporary fix because the leak recurs.
records.solution: Replace the condenser with an improved unit and recharge the system (evacuate, replace the receiver/drier or orifice as needed, pull vacuum, recharge to spec). Confirm the leak with UV dye or an electronic sniffer first — the compressor is usually fine. If within 5yr/60k, pursue Special Coverage 17336 for reimbursement. Common OE-replacement condensers cross to GM3030306 (aftermarket); Denso/ACDelco units are preferred over budget parts that re-crack.
symptoms: A/C blows cold then warm after weeks/months
Oily residue near condenser tube junctions

citations.title: GM Special Coverage 17336 - Air-Conditioning Condenser Refrigerant Leak

records.title: CSFI 'Spider' Central Port Injector / Poppet Valve Failure (5.7L Vortec)
records.description: The 1996-2000 5.7L Vortec (L31) uses a Central Sequential Fuel Injection (CSFI) 'spider' assembly: one central housing feeds six nylon poppet spray nozzles via tubes. The poppet valves gum up with carbon and either stick open (raw fuel dumps, rich condition, hard hot/cold starting, fuel smell) or the plastic tubes crack/leak causing a lean misfire. This is one of the defining driveability failures of the GMT400 Tahoe. GM issued bulletin 87-65-07 and later covered many trucks under an extended emissions warranty for the poppet nozzles.
records.solution: Confirm with a fuel-pressure test and a key-on leak-down check (pressure bleeds off from leaking poppets). The proven fix is replacing the entire spider assembly, ideally upgrading to the later MPFI (multi-point) conversion spider which uses standard injectors instead of poppets and is far more reliable. OEM spider references: GM 25340347 / 17114163; common aftermarket units are sold as 'FJ504' MPFI-style assemblies (roughly $150-400 for the part). Add a fuel filter and clean the throttle body while in there.
symptoms: Loss of power and poor fuel economy

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: CSFI "spider" poppet fuel injector failure (special coverage 99066F)
records.description: The 5.7L, 5.0L and 4.3L Vortec engines used a Central Sequential Fuel Injection (CSFI) "spider" assembly with nylon fuel tubes ending in spring-loaded poppet nozzles inside the intake. The poppets clog with carbon or leak/stick open, causing raw fuel intrusion, hard starting/flooding, and misfires. GM acknowledged the problem with special coverage 99066F on 1996-2003 CSFI systems (emissions-related, extending injector warranty to 10 years/200,000 miles for cleaning or replacement).
records.solution: Diagnose with a fuel-pressure gauge (pressure that bleeds down after shutoff points to leaking poppets). Replace the spider/CSFI assembly. A common permanent fix is to install the later multi-port (MPFI/MFI) spider upgrade used on 2002+ Vortec engines, which drops into 1996-2001 engines and eliminates the poppet design. Check GM special coverage 99066F eligibility.
symptoms: Loss of power and poor fuel economy

records.title: Distributor cap and rotor moisture corrosion (frequent replacement)
records.description: The 1996-1999 Vortec's distributor sits nearly vertical, and its ventilation design allows moisture and condensation to accumulate inside the cap. This causes corrosion, carbon tracking, and cracking of the cap and rotor, producing intermittent misfires and stalling, especially in damp conditions. It is common enough that owners report replacing the cap and rotor roughly annually, and aftermarket ignition parts tend to fail faster than AC Delco/GM originals.
records.solution: Replace the distributor cap and rotor, using OEM AC Delco parts for longevity. Clean the small distributor housing vent holes with compressed air or a thin wire so condensation can escape. Inspect and replace corroded plug wires as needed.
symptoms: Rough running, especially when damp or cold
Corrosion or carbon tracking inside cap

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: EBCM / ABS Module Failure & Corroded Ground (ABS, Traction, StabiliTrak Lights)
records.description: GMT800 Tahoes commonly light the ABS, Traction Control and (on later trucks) StabiliTrak warnings simultaneously due to the Electronic Brake Control Module (EBCM) or, very often, its corroded frame-mounted ground. The dedicated EBCM ground on the driver-side frame rail is exposed to road salt and corrodes, causing intermittent module communication loss and codes like C0265. Internal EBCM solder-joint failures also occur. Normal service braking still works, but ABS/traction functions drop out.
records.solution: Pull chassis 'C' codes first. Before condemning the module, locate and clean/re-terminate the EBCM ground on the frame rail (a cheap, common fix). If the module itself is at fault (C0265/C0110 with confirmed internal fault), options are a rebuild/repair service for the EBCM or a replacement module that must be programmed to the VIN. Inspect the wheel-speed sensor circuits as well. Ground repair can be under $100; module rebuild/replacement runs several hundred.
symptoms: ABS, Traction and StabiliTrak lights on together
Code C0265 / loss of module communication
ABS inoperative but normal pedal braking
Intermittent lights that come and go over bumps

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Exterior Door Handle Cracking / Breaking Off (GMT900)
records.description: The 2007+ GMT900 Tahoe's outside door handles are a notorious weak point. The plastic mounting bosses/studs behind the handle crack and break, so the handle goes loose, rattles, or pulls partway off and won't open the door. A GM bulletin attributes chrome-handle cracking to assembly grease migrating into the screw bosses combined with too-high assembly torque initiating cracks. It commonly hits multiple doors over time and is one of the most-searched GMT900 annoyances.
records.solution: Replace the affected exterior door handle assembly; the trim panel comes off to access it. OEM handles are available but still use the same plastic design; many owners use reinforced aftermarket handles (Dorman offers direct-fit front/rear handles) for durability. Budget roughly $30-90 per handle plus ~30-45 minutes labor each. Doing all four proactively is common on high-mileage trucks.
symptoms: Loose or rattling exterior door handle
Handle pulls out partway but won't open door

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Fuel Level Sensor / Sending Unit Failure (Erratic Fuel Gauge)
records.description: The in-tank fuel-level sender's resistive card wears, causing the fuel gauge to read inaccurately — stuck on Empty or Full, bouncing/fluctuating, or dropping to E with a false low-fuel warning. The sender is integral to the fuel pump module, so a worn card typically means dropping the tank. It is a well-known GM truck problem; on high-mileage trucks technicians recommend replacing the complete fuel pump module rather than just the sender.
records.solution: First rule out a blown fuel-gauge/sender fuse and attempt a scan-tool sensor recalibration. If the gauge is still erratic, replace the fuel level sending unit — on high-mileage trucks replace the complete in-tank fuel pump module (ACDelco/Delphi module) since the pump often follows. Requires dropping the fuel tank.
symptoms: Fuel gauge stuck on E or F

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: GMT900 Cracked Dashboard (Instrument Panel Splitting)
records.description: The molded plastic dashboard on GMT900-platform Tahoes develops long stress cracks in remarkably consistent locations: to the left of the instrument cluster on the driver side and around the passenger airbag seam near the center of the dash. Owners across all climates report the same pattern, pointing to a material/manufacturing defect (cheap plastic substrate and, per some analyses, over-torqued mounting bolts) rather than sun exposure alone. Because the cracks originate at the passenger airbag deployment seam, plaintiffs in a multi-state class action (E.D. Michigan, 2018) alleged a safety risk during airbag deployment. The court ruled in GM's favor in 2019, so there is no recall or warranty remedy and owners bear the repair cost.
records.solution: GM offers no factory fix. Options: (1) full instrument-panel pad replacement at a dealer/body shop (most expensive, cracks often return with OE part); (2) a molded ABS dash cap/overlay bonded over the original (e.g. DashSkin or Coverlay), the most popular durable DIY fix at ~$150-400; (3) a dash cover mat as a cosmetic-only band-aid. Verify any airbag-seam integrity if the crack runs through the passenger airbag deployment door.
symptoms: Long crack to the left of the gauge cluster
Crack around the passenger airbag seam
Sharp raised plastic edges along the crack

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: HVAC Blend / Mode Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Behind Dash)
records.description: The small electric HVAC door actuators use plastic internal gears that strip, crack, or lose calibration. When they fail you get a repetitive clicking or tapping noise from behind the dash (often behind the glove box or center console) that frequently repeats when you change temperature or mode. A stuck door causes classic split-temperature symptoms — hot air from one side and cold from the other — or air stuck coming from the wrong vents (defrost only). Dual-zone and rear-climate Tahoes have multiple actuators, so isolating the noisy/stuck one matters.
records.solution: Replace the failed actuator (temperature/blend, mode, or recirculation) and recalibrate by cycling the ignition/HVAC. For GMT800/GMT900 trucks the common blend/mode-door actuator is ACDelco 15-73952 / GM 52495593 (Dorman equivalent 604-112). Recalibrate per procedure after install; if gears merely lost sync a scan-tool relearn can sometimes clear it without parts.
symptoms: One side hot, other side cold

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Knock Sensor Corrosion / Water Intrusion Under Intake (P0327 & P0332)
records.description: On Gen III/IV small-block V8s the two knock sensors sit down in a recessed valley UNDER the intake manifold. Water (rain, car washes, snow melt) collects in the recess and corrodes the sensors and their two-wire harness, setting P0327 (Bank 1 low) and/or P0332 (Bank 2 low), often together, illuminating the Check Engine light. The ECM then pulls timing, which can cost power and mpg. Because the sensors are buried, this is a heavily searched, labor-intensive nuisance code.
records.solution: Replace BOTH knock sensors AND both wiring harnesses (a partial repair usually returns the code). OEM sensor: ACDelco 213-3521 (GM 12589867). Harness kit: Dorman 917-033 (replaces GM 12601822). This requires removing the intake manifold, so replace the intake manifold gaskets at the same time. GM's procedure calls for building an RTV 'dam' under the sensors to divert water away, and torquing the intake to inch-pounds. Parts run ~$60-150; the labor to pull the intake is the bulk of the cost.
symptoms: Slight loss of power / reduced fuel economy

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Lower Intake Manifold Gasket Coolant Leak (Dex-Cool Erosion)
records.description: Vortec V8 Tahoes are well known for lower intake manifold gasket leaks, most often at the driver-side rear corner coolant passages. Dex-Cool (orange) coolant is hard on these gaskets, softening/distorting them and eroding the aluminum sealing surface, allowing coolant to weep externally or into the lifter valley/oil. It typically starts as a slow leak: a recurring 'Low Coolant' light and a sweet smell, worsening over time and risking overheating or oil contamination if ignored.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system to confirm the intake gasket as the leak source (vs. water pump). Replace the intake manifold gaskets with updated design gaskets, clean/inspect the aluminum sealing surfaces, and torque the intake bolts to spec (inch-pounds, correct sequence). Many owners flush the Dex-Cool and switch to a conventional green coolant as a preventive measure. Do the knock sensors/harness at the same time since the intake is already off. Typical shop cost ~$880-1,050.
symptoms: External coolant weep at rear of intake
Coolant in oil / milky oil (severe cases)

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Lower intake manifold gasket coolant/vacuum leak (5.7L Vortec)
records.description: The 1996-1999 5.7L Vortec (L31) and 5.0L Vortec (L30) used a plastic-carrier composite lower intake manifold gasket that degrades and fails, typically between 60,000-120,000 miles. Failures commonly occur at the coolant ports and near the valley/distributor area, letting coolant seep externally, into the oil, or into the intake, and creating vacuum leaks. GM's light inch-pound torque spec contributed to uneven clamping and premature failure. This is one of the most widely reported problems on this generation truck.
records.solution: Replace the lower intake manifold gasket set, ideally with the upgraded Fel-Pro steel-carrier gasket (MS98000T family) rather than the OEM composite unit, and follow the correct inch-pound torque sequence. Inspect coolant for oil contamination and change oil afterward if coolant intrusion occurred. Replacing the plastic coolant temp sensor and distributor O-ring while the manifold is off is common practice.
symptoms: Low coolant warning / disappearing coolant with no visible puddle
Coolant or oil around the intake manifold

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: 'Reduced Engine Power' Limp Mode - Electronic Throttle (TAC) System
records.description: Tahoes with drive-by-wire throttle (APP pedal sensor + TAC module + electronic throttle body) commonly trigger a 'Reduced Engine Power' message and drop into limp mode with severely limited acceleration - a safety concern in traffic. On GMT800s the frequent culprits are a broken/chafed wire in the throttle-body harness (often the yellow wire), corroded engine grounds, or a dirty/sticking throttle body (P1516/P1515). GMT900s see similar throttle-actuator/APP faults (P2101/P2135/P0120 family).
records.solution: Retrieve codes to isolate the branch: P1515/P1516 point at the TAC/throttle actuator, P2135/P0120-series at the TPS/APP correlation. Start with the cheap, common causes: clean the electronic throttle body, inspect and repair the throttle-body wiring harness (especially chafed/broken wires) and clean/tighten engine grounds. If the throttle body's internal TPS is faulty, replace the electronic throttle body assembly (ACDelco units available; part roughly $120-300). A failed APP pedal sensor is a less common cause.
symptoms: Limp mode / severe loss of acceleration
Check Engine light with throttle codes
Intermittent power loss that clears on restart

citations.title: GM Preliminary Information PIP4578B - Throttle-Body Carbon and Idle Learn

records.title: In-tank fuel pump failure and pigtail connector meltdown
records.description: The in-tank electric fuel pump on the GMT400 Tahoe is a common wear-out item, often failing around/after 100,000 miles. Continuous-duty operation, chronic low-fuel driving (which reduces pump cooling), and tank sediment clogging the sock filter all shorten pump life. A frequently overlooked contributor is the fuel pump wiring harness pigtail/ground connection ahead of the rear axle, which corrodes and melts, causing intermittent power loss to the pump. Skipping the recommended 30,000-mile fuel filter interval accelerates pump failure.
records.solution: Replace the in-tank fuel pump module. Replace the fuel filter and the harness pigtail connector at the same time, and verify/repair the rear ground. Maintain the fuel filter on a 30,000-mile interval and avoid habitually running the tank near empty.

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: In-Tank Fuel Pump Module Failure (Long Crank / No-Start)
records.description: The GMT800 Tahoe's in-tank electric fuel pump module is a common high-mileage failure. As the pump wears it struggles to build and hold the ~58-62 PSI these returnless systems need, producing extended cranking (worst after the truck sits overnight), stalling, hesitation under load, and eventually a crank-but-no-start with no pump 'prime' hum at key-on. Tank contamination/rust and heat accelerate the failure.
records.solution: Confirm with a fuel-pressure gauge on the Schrader port: good pressure should reach ~58-62 PSI within ~2 seconds of key-on and hold. Also check the fuel-pump relay/fuse and inspect the pump connector for heat damage. Fix is a complete fuel pump module (pump + level sender + strainer). OEM: ACDelco MU1613 (GM 19153711), which includes the seal, float and harness; quality aftermarket options include Delphi/Spectra modules (part roughly $150-350). Drop the tank, replace the module and strainer, and blow out/inspect the tank if rust is present.
symptoms: Extended cranking before start, worse after sitting
Crank but no-start with no pump hum at key-on

records.title: Upper Intermediate Steering Shaft Clunk (I-Shaft)
records.description: The upper intermediate steering shaft (I-shaft) between the steering column and the gearbox develops dry, corroded splines that bind and then slip, producing a clunk or knock felt in the steering wheel when turning at low speed or driving over bumps. GM issued TSB 00-02-35-003M acknowledging the condition on Tahoe/Suburban. Greasing the splines is only a temporary fix; the clunk reliably returns.
records.solution: Replace the upper intermediate steering shaft assembly (GM PN 19153614; Dorman/aftermarket equivalents available) for a permanent fix. GM also offers a spline lube kit (PN 26098419) that repacks the splines as a lower-cost repair, but the shaft replacement is the durable remedy per the TSB.
symptoms: Clunk/knock in steering wheel when turning
Clunk over bumps or driveway transitions
Noise from under hood near firewall

records.title: VVT Cam Phaser / Timing Chain Cold-Start Rattle (5.3L)
records.description: Gen V 5.3L engines use variable valve timing (VVT) with a cam phaser and VVT solenoid. Sludge and wear cause the phaser to rattle and the timing chain to stretch, producing a cold-start 'marbles in a can' rattle that often precedes a check-engine light. It sets crank/cam correlation codes (P0008/P0016/P0017) or VVT performance codes (P0011). GM TSB PIP5921B also documents a rattle/tick from the intake cam actuator when its cover-plate screws back out. Ignored, a stretched chain can jump timing and cause severe internal damage.
records.solution: Diagnose early: scan for P0008/P0016/P0017/P0011 and inspect actual-vs-desired cam angle. Replace the VVT solenoid(s) and, if the chain has stretched or the phaser rattles, replace the timing chain, cam phaser and tensioner as a set. Address the underlying oil sludge (correct dexos oil and shorter change intervals). Do not dismiss a cold-start rattle as normal — it is often the first sign of a stretching chain.
symptoms: Cold-start rattle for a few seconds

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: Water Pump Failure / Coolant Leak
records.description: The engine-driven water pump bearing and shaft seal wear out, leaking coolant from the weep hole and eventually letting the impeller wobble or the bearing seize. Coolant loss leads to overheating if ignored. It's a routine wear item on the small-block V8s, commonly needed around/after 100k miles — and some replacement pumps of poor quality fail far sooner, so pump quality matters.
records.solution: Replace the water pump with an OE-quality unit (ACDelco / GM Genuine or Aisin/Gates equivalent) and fresh dexos-approved coolant; inspect the belt, tensioner and thermostat while there. Avoid the cheapest pumps — some last only ~30k miles versus 100k+ for a quality unit. Pressure-test the system afterward to confirm no residual leaks.
symptoms: Coolant puddle / drip from front of engine
Whine or wobble from pump bearing

records.title: Worn Steering Gearbox - Sector Shaft Play & Seal Leak (Loose/Wandering Steering)
records.description: The recirculating-ball steering gearbox on GMT800 Tahoes becomes notoriously sloppy with mileage. Internal wear of the worm/sector gear and bearings produces excessive on-center steering play, vague/wandering tracking at highway speed, and a clunk, while the sector-shaft (pitman) output seal weeps power-steering fluid down the box. It's a very common high-mileage complaint and a safety/handling concern distinct from the intermediate-shaft clunk.
records.solution: Distinguish gearbox wear from worn intermediate shaft, idler/pitman arms, and tie-rod ends (get the truck on a lift and check for play at each). A gearbox with an over-center adjustment can sometimes be snugged to reduce on-center play, but a badly worn or leaking box should be replaced with a quality remanufactured unit (ACDelco or Lares reman gearbox; part roughly $150-350) plus an alignment afterward. Replacing the pitman-shaft seals is possible but usually the whole box is swapped on high-mileage trucks.
symptoms: Vehicle wanders / needs constant correction at speed
Clunk when turning or over bumps
Power-steering fluid leak at the gearbox

records.title: 4WD Actuator Motor Failure
records.description: Electric 4WD engagement actuator on transfer case fails, preventing 4WD engagement. Actuator motor burns out or connector corrodes.
records.solution: Replace transfer case actuator motor. Clean and protect electrical connector with dielectric grease. Test 4WD engagement monthly to keep actuator exercised.

records.title: Rear Differential Pinion Seal Leak
records.description: Rear differential pinion seal leaks gear oil onto driveshaft and exhaust. Can drip onto hot exhaust components causing burning smell and smoke.
records.solution: Replace pinion seal. Check pinion bearing preload and bearing condition while seal is removed. Top off differential with correct gear oil.

records.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure
records.description: Timing chain tensioner fails allowing chain to slap and jump timing. 2.5L V6 particularly susceptible. Can cause valve damage if chain jumps more than one tooth.
records.solution: Replace timing chain, tensioner, and guides as a kit. Check for valve damage on V6 if chain has jumped. This is a significant repair on the V6 due to tight engine bay.
symptoms: Engine will not start if chain jumped

records.title: 4.2L I6 Coolant Leak from Throttle Body and Water Pump
records.description: The 4.2L Atlas I6 develops coolant leaks from the throttle body heater port, water pump weep hole, and thermostat housing. These are progressive leaks that worsen over time.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the throttle body heater hoses/port, thermostat housing, and the water pump weep hole on the 4.2L Atlas I6; dried coolant residue below the pump pulley or around the throttle body usually confirms the source. Replace any leaking throttle body heater hose or fitting, the thermostat housing and seal if seepage is present, and the water pump if coolant is coming from the weep hole; on these engines it is also wise to install a new thermostat and fresh Dex-Cool coolant during service. After repair, vacuum-fill or properly bleed the system and verify fan clutch operation and operating temperature on a road test. Typical repair cost ranges from about $150-$300 for hoses or housing repairs, and roughly $500-$900 for a water pump replacement depending on labor rates and parts quality.

records.title: CVT Transmission Shudder and Hesitation
records.description: The Trailblazer with the 1.2L turbo and CVT automatic develops shudder during light acceleration and hesitation from stops. Some owners report a rubber-band feel typical of CVT calibration issues.

citations.title: GM Preliminary Information PIP6036B - CVT Surge or Fishbite Diagnostic Aid

records.title: Electric Fan Clutch Failure
records.description: The TrailBlazer uses an electronically controlled viscous fan clutch that fails, causing overheating in traffic or when towing. A failed fan clutch can also cause excessive fan engagement, creating a loud roaring noise and reduced fuel economy.
records.solution: Confirm fan clutch operation with a scan tool by comparing commanded fan speed to actual speed and checking for related DTCs such as P1481, P1482, P1484, or P0526, then inspect the fan clutch harness and connector for oil contamination or damaged wiring. If the clutch is stuck engaged, freewheeling, or not responding to PCM commands, replace the electronic viscous fan clutch assembly; on many TrailBlazers this is a bolt-on repair requiring fan shroud removal and a special fan clutch wrench/holding tool. After replacement, clear codes, verify fan engagement during warm idle and A/C operation, and confirm coolant temperature stays stable in traffic. Typical repair cost is about $300-$700 total depending on brand of clutch and labor time, with OEM-quality parts strongly recommended.

records.title: Turbocharger Oil Leak and Failure
records.description: The 1.2L and 1.3L turbocharged three-cylinder engines in the Trailblazer can develop turbo oil seal leaks, causing oil consumption and blue smoke on startup. The turbo oil feed and return lines are also prone to seepage. In severe cases, the turbo can fail completely.
records.solution: Replace turbo oil feed and return line seals first. If the turbo itself is leaking internally, turbocharger replacement is required. Use only GM-spec synthetic oil to minimize carbon buildup on turbo seals.
symptoms: Turbo whistle or whine changes pitch
Check engine light for boost-related codes

citations.title: GM Special Coverage N242484750 - 1.2L Turbocharger Replacement

records.title: 1.2L/1.3L Turbo Engine Oil Consumption
records.description: The small-displacement turbo engines in the Trailblazer can consume oil between changes, particularly the 1.2L 3-cylinder. Some owners report needing to add oil between the 7,500-mile change intervals.
symptoms: Oil consumption above 1 qt per 2000 miles

records.title: Power Window Regulator Failure
records.description: The cable-style window regulators in 2002-2009 TrailBlazers fail frequently. The plastic guide portion breaks, cables fray and wrap around the motor pulley, or the motor gears strip. Windows move slowly, make grinding/clicking noises, or become stuck. The front windows are most commonly affected. Lack of lubrication and debris in window tracks accelerate wear.
symptoms: Grinding or clicking noise when operating window
Window stuck in up or down position
Motor runs but window does not move

records.title: 9-Speed Automatic (9T65) Torque Converter Shudder on Low-Speed Shifts
records.description: Second-generation Traverse models paired the 3.6L LFY V6 with GM's 9T65 9-speed automatic, which exhibits a noticeable shudder/shake felt during 1-2, 2-3 and 3-4 upshifts at speeds below ~40 mph under light-to-moderate throttle. GM traced it to torque converter clutch (TCC) re-apply shudder after a shift, accelerated by degraded factory transmission fluid. Left unaddressed, the friction material in the converter wears further and eventually requires converter replacement.
records.solution: Per GM preliminary bulletin, perform a full transmission fluid exchange with fresh DEXRON VI (later guidance specifies Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP), reprogram the TCM with the latest calibration, run the Service Fast Learn procedure, and road-test a minimum of 200 miles. A fluid flush caught early permanently eliminates the shudder; if friction material is already worn, the torque converter must be replaced.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration felt during 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 upshifts
Shaking under light throttle below 40 mph
Sensation like driving over rumble strips during acceleration
No shudder under hard throttle or at higher gears

citations.title: GM Service Bulletin 18-NA-091 - Low-Speed 9T65 TCC Shudder

records.title: 9-Speed Automatic Transmission Shudder (9T65)
records.description: The second-generation Traverse (2018+) uses the GM 9T65 9-speed automatic transmission that suffers from a shudder during light acceleration in the 25-50 mph range. The torque converter clutch chatters during lockup, producing a vibration that feels like driving on a rumble strip. The 9-speed also exhibits harsh downshifts, hunting between gears on hills, and delayed engagement from Park. GM has released multiple TCM software updates to address the shifting behavior, but the underlying torque converter weakness remains.
records.solution: Start with a dealer visit for the latest TCM software calibration — GM has released numerous updates that improve 9-speed behavior. A full transmission fluid exchange with Mobil 1 LV ATF HP (DEXRON HP specification) can significantly reduce or eliminate the shudder. If both steps fail, the torque converter needs replacement ($1,500-$2,500 including labor). Some owners have had success with a complete transmission replacement under warranty. Change the 9T65 fluid every 45,000 miles as preventive maintenance.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration at 25-50 mph under light throttle
Transmission hunting between gears on hills
Delayed engagement from Park to Drive
Hesitation on acceleration from low speeds

records.title: AC Compressor Premature Failure
records.description: The Traverse has one of the highest rates of AC compressor failure among midsize SUVs. Compressors seize or lose capacity often before 70,000 miles. When the compressor fails, it can send metal debris through the entire AC system, requiring replacement of the condenser, expansion valve, and system flush. Some owners report repeat failures within 8 months of repair.
records.solution: Confirm the failure by checking static and running refrigerant pressures, verifying compressor clutch command/power and ground, and inspecting for noise, seizure, or metal contamination in the oil and lines. If the compressor has failed internally, replace the compressor, receiver/drier or condenser assembly (the drier is integrated on many GM systems), expansion valve/orifice components as applicable, thoroughly flush any reusable lines and evaporator, evacuate the system, and recharge with the exact specified refrigerant and PAG oil; also inspect cooling fan operation and high-side pressures so an overpressure condition does not destroy the replacement unit. If debris is present, a simple compressor swap often leads to repeat failure, so a full system cleanout is the correct repair. Typical cost is about $1,200-$2,500 for a complete repair depending on how many contaminated components must be replaced.
symptoms: Clicking or grinding noise from compressor

citations.title: NHTSA Manufacturer Communications Data Corpus

records.title: A/C Evaporator Core Leak
records.description: The first-generation Traverse (2009-2017) develops A/C evaporator leaks that cause loss of refrigerant and warm air from the vents. The evaporator core, located inside the dashboard HVAC housing, corrodes internally due to moisture and acid buildup from the refrigerant-oil mixture. The leak is slow enough that the A/C may work fine early in summer but gradually loses cooling as refrigerant escapes over weeks. The evaporator is extremely labor-intensive to access, making this one of the most expensive A/C repairs.
records.solution: The evaporator core must be replaced, which requires removing the entire dashboard assembly to access the HVAC housing — 8-12 hours of labor ($800-$1,500). The evaporator core itself costs $100-$300. Also replace the expansion valve and receiver/drier while the system is apart ($50-$100 additional). Total repair: $1,200-$2,500. As a temporary fix, a refrigerant recharge with UV dye ($100-$200) will restore cooling for weeks to months, but the leak will return. Always check for evaporator leaks before spending money on other A/C diagnostics.
symptoms: A/C blows warm air gradually over weeks
A/C works after recharge but fails again
Musty smell from vents (moisture from leak)
A/C low pressure reading with no visible leak

records.title: Airbags May Not Deploy - SDM Left in Manufacturing Mode (Recall 18V774000)
records.description: NHTSA recall 18V774000 (GM campaign 18365) covers certain 2019 Traverse vehicles (and sibling Encore/Spark/Trax) whose Sensing Diagnostic Module (SDM) was never switched out of factory 'manufacturing mode' before shipment. With the SDM in this state the airbags will not deploy in a crash, and seatbelt reminders, event data recording, and automatic post-crash notification are also inactive — a serious occupant-protection defect even though only a small build window was affected.
records.solution: Take the vehicle to a Chevrolet dealer to have the SDM reprogrammed to the correct operating mode free of charge under recall 18365 / NHTSA 18V774000. Owners can verify their VIN's recall status on NHTSA's site or by calling Chevrolet at 1-800-222-1020. No parts replacement is required — it is a software/configuration fix.
symptoms: Airbag warning light behavior may appear normal yet airbags are disabled

citations.title: GM Recall 18365 / NHTSA 18V-774 - SDM Manufacturing Mode

records.title: A/C Condenser / Refrigerant Line Leak Causing Loss of Cooling
records.description: Traverse owners widely report the air conditioning blowing warm air after only a year or two of use, caused by refrigerant escaping the system. GM bulletin PIT5710 instructs dealers to leak-check the condenser and, if no external leak is found, inspect the rear auxiliary A/C evaporator. The condenser itself is alleged to be defectively manufactured, and the aluminum tube can separate from or rupture at the rubber hose between the compressor and condenser — the same defect at the center of a GM class-action lawsuit covering Traverse and sibling SUVs.
records.solution: Have the system evacuated and dye/pressure leak-tested. Common fixes are replacing the condenser (or the compressor-to-condenser line) and recharging the system; if the leak is internal, the rear auxiliary evaporator is replaced. Upgraded condenser part designs are used on repairs. Repair commonly runs $500-$1,400 depending on whether the condenser, line, or evaporator is at fault.
symptoms: Cooling fails again shortly after a recharge

records.title: EVAP Purge Valve Failure Causing Rough Idle, Stalling and Hard Starts (P0496) — GM Special Coverage N232395300
records.description: On the 3.6L V6 (RPO LFY) Traverse, the evaporative emissions purge valve can fail to fully close, allowing fuel vapor to flood the intake. This causes a P0496 (EVAP high purge flow) code with rough running, hesitation, or stalling at idle, and hard starting after refueling. GM acknowledged the condition and issued Special Coverage N232395300 (15 years / 150,000 miles) to replace the purge valve at no charge on affected 2019 Traverse units.
records.solution: Replace the failed evaporative emission purge/solenoid valve (free under GM Special Coverage N232395300 on eligible 2019 3.6L units); clear P0496 and verify EVAP system seal. Check for related EVAP codes (P0442, P0455) that can accompany the failure.
symptoms: Rough idle or stalling at idle

citations.title: GM Special Coverage N232395300 - Evaporative Emissions Purge Valve

records.title: Excessive Oil Consumption on 3.6L LFY (Worn Rings / PCV)
records.description: Second-generation Traverse owners report the 3.6L LFY V6 consuming oil at roughly 1 quart every 1,000-2,000 miles, with some AWD examples burning a half-quart per 1,000 miles starting around 55k miles. Root causes are worn/coked piston rings and a PCV system that pulls oil vapor into the intake. Because there is often no visible leak, owners discover it only when the low-oil light comes in or the engine runs low between changes, risking accelerated wear if not topped up.
records.solution: Document consumption with a dealer oil-consumption test (GM now considers worse than ~1 qt/2,000 miles excessive). Early-stage cases sometimes improve by replacing the PCV valve/connector; confirmed ring wear requires teardown and ring/piston service or a short block. Interim management is checking the dipstick at every fuel stop and topping up with the correct dexos1 0W-20/5W-30.
symptoms: Low oil level / oil light between changes
Needing to add oil every 1,000-2,000 miles
Occasional blue-gray exhaust smoke on startup

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure — Warm Air on One Side / Inconsistent Dual-Zone Temps
records.description: The dual-zone climate system on the Traverse commonly suffers blend door actuator failures, where one side (often the passenger side or rear) blows warm air while the other blows cold regardless of temperature setting. The plastic gears inside the actuator strip or stick, often producing a clicking/knocking sound from behind the dash; this is a recurring complaint shared across GM models with split climate control.
records.solution: Diagnose and replace the failed HVAC blend door actuator(s) for the affected zone, then recalibrate the climate system. A clicking/knocking sound from behind the dash typically indicates actuator gear failure.
symptoms: Warm air from one side while the other is cold
Rear or passenger zone won't change temperature
Clicking or knocking noise behind the dashboard
Climate control not matching set temperature
